# Albany, NY to New York City, NY Passenger Rail Corridor Proposal

> **Illustrative estimates: costs, schedules and funding figures in this draft come from an uncalibrated planning model and approximate program parameters. They are not budgets or engineering estimates.**

## Executive Summary

This proposal evaluates three conceptual alternatives for passenger rail service between Albany, NY and New York City, NY based on 5000 simulation runs per alternative. The options include Alternative 1 (Existing corridor upgrade), Alternative 2 (New direct alignment), and Alternative 3 (Via intermediate cities). Each alternative serves 3 stations in route order: Albany, Poughkeepsie, and New York City.

Alternative 1 yields the lowest median (P50) cost at $6.1B and the shortest median (P50) time to opening at 11.0 years. Alternative 2 provides the shortest route at 140 miles but requires higher capital investment, while Alternative 3 offers an intermediate configuration. Population figures reflect 2020 Census residents within 10 miles of the line and do not represent passenger ridership forecasts.

## Corridor Description

Alternative 1 (Existing corridor upgrade) covers 145 miles with 98.7% of its path on existing rail right-of-way and requires 2 miles of new track. It records 6 environmental flag entries, 13 river crossings, and 0 miles of new track in flagged areas. It places 12.21 million residents near the alignment and 4.38 million residents near stations.

Alternative 2 (New direct alignment) spans 140 miles, utilizing a 24.4% share on existing rail corridors alongside 106 miles of new track. It includes 1 environmental flag entry, 1 river crossing, and 0 miles of new track in flagged areas. This alignment has 12.17 million residents near the alignment and 4.38 million residents near stations.

Alternative 3 (Via intermediate cities) extends 160 miles with a 48.2% share on existing rail corridors and 83 miles of new track. It records 2 environmental flag entries, 2 river crossings, and 2 miles of new track in flagged areas, serving 12.12 million residents near the alignment and 4.38 million residents near stations.

## Cost and Schedule Range

Costs discussed in this proposal are illustrative estimates, not project budgets. For Alternative 1, the capital cost ranges from a P10 of $5.0B to a P90 of $7.6B, with a median (P50) of $6.1B. The projected time to opening for Alternative 1 is a P10 of 9.5 years, a median (P50) of 11.0 years, and a P90 of 12.6 years.

For Alternative 2, the capital cost spans a P10 of $7.8B to a P90 of $10.9B, with a median (P50) of $9.2B. Its time to opening is modeled at a P10 of 11.3 years, a median (P50) of 12.8 years, and a P90 of 14.5 years.

For Alternative 3, the capital cost spans a P10 of $7.7B to a P90 of $10.9B, with a median (P50) of $9.2B. The time to opening for Alternative 3 is estimated at a P10 of 10.9 years, a median (P50) of 12.4 years, and a P90 of 14.0 years.

## Funding Strategy

All three alternatives align with the Corridor Identification and Development Program (Corridor ID) for planning grants, providing $500K in federal funding with a fit score of 0.95. The primary capital funding opportunity across all options is the Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (National) grant, which offers up to $3.0B per award. This grant covers 48.8% of the median (P50) cost for Alternative 1, 32.4% for Alternative 2, and 32.7% for Alternative 3.

Additional federal programs include CRISI grants capped near $250M (covering 4.1% of median cost for Alternative 1, and 2.7% for Alternatives 2 and 3) and BUILD grants capped at $25M. Alternative 1 also matches the Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (Northeast Corridor) program for $246M (4.0% of median cost). To cover non-federal match requirements, RRIF loans could provide $1.2B for Alternative 1 or $1.8B for Alternatives 2 and 3, contingent on identifying a dedicated repayment source.

## Risks

Risk factors and key technical considerations for the corridor alternatives include:
* Constructing new track, particularly the 106 miles in Alternative 2 or the 83 miles in Alternative 3, increases land acquisition and delivery complexity.
* Navigating environmental constraints, including 13 river crossings under Alternative 1 and 2 miles of new track in flagged areas under Alternative 3.
* Securing host railroad agreements; presence on an existing rail corridor does not establish track ownership access, spare capacity, or operating permission.

## Next Steps

To advance corridor planning, state DOT planners should address unmodeled items in future study phases:
* Develop detailed ridership, station-pair demand forecasts, and door-to-door travel time competitiveness analyses.
* Model track capacity, freight conflicts, train paths, and negotiate access agreements with host railroads.
* Evaluate service frequency, timetables, span of service, on-time performance, and reliability targets.
* Complete fleet planning for rolling stock, maintenance facilities, and electrification requirements.
* Conduct full financial and benefit-cost analyses, including operating and maintenance costs, fare revenue, operating subsidies, emissions, and safety outcomes.
